title: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (18–25 January)
hookLine: Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants pray together
tomorrow: The Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January)

cards: Picture a small town with three churches on the same street: a Catholic parish, a Lutheran church, a Greek Orthodox church with a dome.
Most weeks they run their own schedules, ring their own bells, hold their own bake sales. Then, for one week in January, the doors open sideways. The Lutheran pastor reads at the Catholic Vespers.
The Catholic choir sings in the Orthodox church. Someone brings coffee for everyone. It has a name, and a start date: January 18.

teach.b: On the night before he died, John's gospel says, Jesus prayed for his followers, and for those who would believe through them: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee."
Within a few centuries the followers had split, and split again: East and West in the Middle Ages, then the Reformation in the West.
In 1908, Father Paul Wattson, an Episcopal priest in New York who had founded a community of friars at Graymoor, began an octave of prayer for Christian unity.
The next year he and his community were received into the Catholic Church, and popes encouraged the octave.
In the 1930s a French priest, Abbé Paul Couturier, widened it: pray for the unity Christ wills, by the means he wills, so Christians of every church could join without first agreeing on the details.

Since 1968, Catholics and the World Council of Churches, which includes many Orthodox and Protestant churches, have prepared the prayers together each year, often written by Christians in a different country.
The dates come from an older calendar, from a feast of Peter on January 18 to the conversion of Paul on January 25; in the southern hemisphere, many churches keep the week around Pentecost instead.
The Second Vatican Council called this kind of shared prayer the soul of the whole effort toward unity.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: Real differences remain, and each church keeps its own teaching. But for eight days, people who disagree about a great deal stand in the same room and pray the same Our Father.

how: From January 18 to 25 (or around Pentecost in parts of the southern hemisphere), many Catholic parishes join other churches for shared prayer services using materials prepared jointly by the Vatican and the World Council of Churches.

games.q: it's 1908. you're Father Paul Wattson, choosing eight days to pray for Christian unity. which dates do you pick?
o: a feast of Peter on January 18 to Paul's conversion on January 25.
games.why: Peter to Paul: in the calendar of the day, January 18 was a feast of Peter's chair and January 25 the conversion of Paul.

practice: If you're Christian, think of someone from a different church, a Baptist cousin, an Orthodox coworker, a Catholic neighbor, and hold them in mind through one slow Our Father.

If you're not Christian, think of one person on the other side of a divide in your own life, and hold them without arguing in your head. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own words, that they may be one.
